newsitem.title: IRAN: Signs Iran turns back on violence abroad - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Signs Iran turns back on violence abroad - analysts.

text.p: Signs are emerging that Iran has
turned its back on violence abroad and is preparing for a more positive role in foreign relations, analysts said on Thursday.

Issues like the Mykonos affair, which has severely strained relations with the European Union over German charges of top Iranian involvement in political assassinations, have shown that a heavy political price can be exacted for the use of violence.
"Violence hasn't paid off. Mykonos must be a trauma for Iran's leaders. They realise it can all come back to haunt you," one Iranian analyst said.

Relations between Iran and the 15 EU countries are tense over a German court verdict implicating top Iranian leaders in the murder of Kurdish dissidents in Berlin's Mykonos restaurant five years ago. Iran has repeatedly denied involvement.
The United States brands Shi'ite Moslem Iran a rogue state that sponsors "terrorism" abroad -- a charge denied by Tehran, which says it has itself been the victim of "terrorism".
"Iran's top leadership has turned its back on violence. The regime's policy is based on expediency and past experience has shown violence has not paid," the Iranian analyst said.

But revolutionary bodies could throw up obstacles in moves towards moderation. The problem was in separating top leaders from control of the activities of such bodies as the 15th Khordad Foundation, Revolutionary Guards and Basij militia.

Supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, in remarks broadcast on Wednesday, said there was no need to export Iran's Islamic revolution -- an accusation often levelled at Tehran by Gulf Arab states nervous about Iran's arms buildup.

In a eulogy marking the anniversary of the death in 1989 of the revolution's founder, Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, he said: "We do not believe in the export of our revolution as the Marxists of the 1950s believed.
"Since our revolution is Islamic all the Moslems in all corners of the world feel a deep affinity for it. This is how our revolution goes to all corners of the world."
Analysts said Khamenei's moderate tone was in tune with the views of President-elect Mohammad Khatami, a clergyman who describes Islam as a religion of dialogue and tolerance.
Khamenei said in March Islam would definitely not be spread throughout the world by political and military pressure.
"God's religion will win the people's hearts. One cannot win hearts by the sword and force of arms. Islam never favoured the use of force," the supreme leader said.
He said Islam had two means by which it could gain victory over all other religions -- strong logic and absolute justice.

Analysts said the emphasis on logic and justice was aimed at those who favoured violence -- especially "terrorism" -- to fight Iran's perceived enemies and marked the beginning of a new discussion in the country's international relations.
They said President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani repeated the same sort of argument at a summit of Moslem states in the Pakistani capital Islamabad in March.
The analysts noted that Khatami, who is due take over from Rafsanjani in August, said earlier this week he disagreed with the concept of the clash of civilisations.
"He's saying 'We are ready for dialogue'," one said.

"This is a new era in Iranian politics. First it was revolution, violence and war. Then came Rafsanjani's era of reconstruction. Both were mobilisation themes. The third era of more positive engagement with the rest of the world has begun."
